title: GEO, AEO and SEO: How to Get Your Brand Cited by AI Search
metaTitle: GEO vs AEO vs SEO: Getting Cited by AI Search | TDM
metaDescription: What GEO and AEO mean, how they differ from SEO, and the practical steps that get a brand quoted in ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI Overviews.
excerpt: Buyers now ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI Overviews for recommendations before they ever see a list of links. Here is what GEO and AEO actually are, how they relate to SEO, and what to change on your site so the answer includes you.

faqs.q: What is the difference between SEO, AEO and GEO?
faqs.a: SEO (search engine optimization) earns rankings in a list of search results. AEO (answer engine optimization) shapes content so a search engine or assistant can lift a direct answer from it, as in featured snippets and voice results. GEO (generative engine optimization) aims to have a brand named or cited inside answers written by AI systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews. They share one foundation: a site that is crawlable, clearly structured and trusted.

No. AI answers are assembled largely from pages that search engines can already find and trust, so a site with weak SEO has little chance of being cited. GEO adds a layer on top: clearer answers, verifiable facts, structured data and mentions of your brand on other sites.

faqs.q: How do I know if AI assistants mention my brand?
faqs.a: Ask them. Put the questions your customers would ask into ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google, in each language you sell in, and record whether you are named, who is named instead, and which sources are cited. Repeat the same questions every month, because answers change. Referral traffic from AI assistants also shows up in analytics as visits from their domains.

faqs.q: Do I need an llms.txt file?
faqs.a: It is optional and cheap to add. An llms.txt file is a plain-text summary of a site and its key pages, written for AI systems. There is no evidence that it is a ranking factor, and not every AI system reads it, so treat it as a tidy extra rather than a strategy. Clear pages, structured data and third-party mentions matter far more.

body:
A few years ago, a buyer looking for an agency, a product or a supplier typed a few words into Google and worked through the links. Today a growing share of them ask a question instead, in ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity or Google's own AI Overviews, and get a written answer that names two or three options. If your brand is not one of them, you were never in the running.

That shift has produced two new acronyms, GEO and AEO, and a lot of confusion about whether SEO still matters. It does. This guide explains what each term means, how they fit together, and what to change on your site.

## What SEO, AEO and GEO each mean

**SEO**, search engine optimization, is the work of earning a place in the list of results a search engine shows: making pages crawlable, relevant to what people search, and trusted enough to rank.

**AEO**, answer engine optimization, focuses on being the source of a direct answer. It started with featured snippets and voice assistants, where the engine reads out one answer instead of showing ten links.

**GEO**, generative engine optimization, is about being named or cited in answers written by AI systems. The answer is composed fresh for each question, drawing on many sources at once.

In practice the three overlap heavily. An AI answer is usually built from pages a search engine has already crawled and judged trustworthy. So the brands that show up in AI answers are, most of the time, brands that already do the basics of [SEO](/marketing/seo/) well.

## How AI systems decide what to cite

No AI company publishes a full rulebook, and the systems change often. But the pattern across them is consistent enough to act on.

- They retrieve pages that match the question, usually through a search index, so pages that cannot be crawled or indexed are invisible.
- They prefer passages that answer the question directly and can be quoted without needing the rest of the page.
- They lean on sources that other sources agree with, so a claim repeated across independent sites carries more weight than one made only on your own.
- They favour specifics: numbers, names, dates, prices and steps, over general statements.

This is why a page that opens with three paragraphs of scene-setting rarely gets quoted, and a page that answers the question in its first two sentences often does.

## Write so a machine can lift the answer

The single most useful habit is to answer the question first, then explain.

Take each important page and ask what question it answers. Put that question in a heading, and answer it in the first one or two sentences underneath, in plain words, in a way that still makes sense if those sentences are quoted alone. Then add the detail.

- Define terms the first time you use them. "Staff augmentation is hiring dedicated team members through a partner who employs and manages them" is quotable. "We offer flexible talent solutions" is not.
- Use real questions as headings, phrased the way customers ask them.
- Put comparisons in a consistent structure, so the differences are easy to extract.
- Add a short FAQ to pages where buyers have predictable questions, and keep the answers honest and specific.
- State facts with their source or their scope: which client, which period, which market.

## Structured data still matters

Structured data, also called schema markup, is code that labels what a page contains: this is an organization, this is a service, this is a question and its answer, this is an article and when it was published. It removes guesswork for any system reading the page.

The types that matter most for a service business are Organization, Service, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, Article or BlogPosting, and LocalBusiness for real offices. Mark up only what is visibly on the page, and keep it accurate. Markup that claims things the page does not show can be ignored or penalised.

## Build proof outside your own site

AI systems, like people, trust what others say about you more than what you say about yourself. Mentions on independent sites are the hardest part of GEO to fake and the most valuable.

- Keep business listings and profiles consistent: the same name, address, phone number and description everywhere.
- Earn reviews on the platforms your buyers use, and respond to them.
- Publish work that others want to reference: original data, detailed case studies, clear guides.
- Get quoted in industry publications and partner sites.

Detailed, verifiable case studies do double duty here. They give a human buyer proof, and they give an AI system specific facts to cite. A claim like "16× organic traffic growth in twelve months for a UAE fragrance retailer" is far more quotable than "we deliver great results".

## Technical basics that decide whether you are even considered

None of the above helps if AI systems and search engines cannot read the site.

- Make sure important pages are indexable, load quickly and work without JavaScript errors.
- Keep a current XML sitemap and submit it in Google Search Console.
- Check robots.txt. Some sites block AI crawlers by accident, or on purpose without weighing the cost.
- Use one clear URL per page, with correct canonical tags, and correct language tags if you publish in several languages.
- Keep content current. Pages with visible, recent dates and up-to-date facts are easier to trust.

If you sell in more than one language, do all of this per language. An Arabic question gets an answer built from Arabic sources, which is one reason [Arabic SEO](/blog/arabic-seo-guide/) is such an open opportunity in the Gulf.

## How to measure it

Measurement for AI search is less mature than for classic SEO, so combine a few signals.

- Run a fixed list of customer questions through the main AI assistants each month and log who is named.
- Watch analytics for referral visits from AI assistants.
- Track branded search volume in Google Search Console. When AI answers mention you, more people search for you by name.
- Keep watching the classic metrics: rankings, organic traffic and leads. They are still where most of the volume is.

## Where to start

If you are starting from zero, do these in order. Fix crawling and indexing problems. Rewrite your top service pages so each answers its main question in the first lines. Add FAQs and structured data. Publish two or three detailed case studies. Then work on mentions and reviews off the site.

This is the same sequence TDM follows for clients, because the people who handle [SEO](/marketing/seo/) work alongside the developers who implement the technical fixes. If you want an honest read on how visible your brand is in AI answers today, [book a free consultation](/contact/).
